categories.description: Choose the matching syntax and comparison rules.
categories.name: Matching

options.summary: Match without regard to case
options.detail: Use -i or its obsolete alias -y. Case-sensitive matching is the default. Some Unicode letters have locale-dependent case relationships.

options.summary: Use extended regular expressions
options.detail: Use -E for alternatives (|) and grouping (parentheses) without backslashes. Quote the expression to pass these characters through the shell.

options.summary: Match literal strings
options.detail: With -F, dots, stars and brackets match themselves anywhere in the line. Both Ubuntu releases also accept the undocumented alias --fixed-regexp.

options.summary: Match whole words
options.detail: With -w, a match must start and end at a line edge or next to a non-word character. Letters, digits and underscores are word characters. Thus cat matches in cat-food but not in cat_food. Whole-line matching (-x) supersedes -w.

options.summary: Select lines matching no pattern
options.detail: With -v, every supplied pattern must fail for the line to be selected. Counts, filename lists and per-file limits use that selection.

options.detail: Without -e or -f, the first operand is the pattern. Use -e '-x' or -- '-x' for a pattern starting with a dash. Repeat -e or -f to search for any of their patterns. Newlines separate patterns, and an empty pattern matches every line by default. With -P, supply one distinct pattern.

options.summary: Use basic regular expressions
options.detail: This is the default syntax (-G). Use \( and \) for grouping and \| for alternatives. Quote the pattern to preserve the backslashes.

options.summary: Match a Perl-compatible regular expression
options.detail: Use -P with a single distinct pattern. In UTF-8, \d matches ASCII digits on both Ubuntu releases. For Unicode decimal digits, use \p{Nd}. [[:digit:]] includes Unicode digits on Resolute (PCRE2 10.46) but only ASCII digits on Noble (10.42). (?-aD) enables Unicode \d with PCRE2 10.43 or later. To match across newlines, use -z and (?s) within a record.

options.summary: Restore case-sensitive matching
options.detail: Overrides a preceding -i or -y. A later -i enables case folding again.

options.summary: Require the pattern to match the whole line
options.detail: Use -x with a fixed string for an exact line or with a regular expression to anchor the entire pattern. With -z the boundary is a NUL-delimited record.

options.summary: Read search patterns from a file
options.detail: Use -f FILE to read one pattern per line, or -f - for standard input. Repeat -f or combine it with -e for alternatives. An empty file supplies no patterns and selects nothing by itself. A blank line supplies an empty pattern, which matches every line by default.

bare.reason: This is a text/selector grammar, not an unsuffixed scalar measurement

forms.grammar: One pattern per line. A dash reads patterns from standard input.

when_absent.meaning: Use the positional pattern or other pattern sources.

options.summary: Select a grep matcher by name
options.detail: Undocumented in both release manuals. Supply the name after -X or attach it directly, as in -Xawk. The grep, egrep and fgrep matchers implement -G, -E and -F. The perl matcher needs PCRE2. The awk, gawk and posixawk matchers select AWK expression dialects. Conflicting matcher selections are rejected.

categories.description: Choose the information printed for matches.
categories.name: Output

options.summary: Prefix output with line numbers
options.detail: With -n, numbering begins at 1 in each input. With -o, several matches on one line carry the same line number.

options.summary: Count selected lines per file
options.detail: With -c, several matches on one line count once. With -v, count lines matching none of the patterns. A count of zero normally gives status 1 when no input had a selected line. Even with -z the count ends in newline.

options.summary: List files with a selected line
options.detail: With -l, print a qualifying file name once. Normally the first selected line is enough. With -v, one nonmatching line qualifies the file. Use -Z to terminate names with NUL.

options.summary: Print each nonempty match separately
options.detail: With -o, empty matches produce no output. Several matches on one line print separately. With -z, each ends in NUL. With -b, the offset identifies the start of each match. Context lines are suppressed, although separators can still appear between groups. Use --no-group-separator to omit these too. With -v, a selected line can give status 0 with no matching piece to print.

Use -C NUM or the historical -NUM form (for example, -3). Explicit -A and -B override their respective sides. The default group separator is a line containing two dashes (--). With -o, grep omits context lines.
options.summary: Show lines before and after each selected line

variants.meaning: Context lines on each side of a match

forms.grammar: Nonnegative base-10 integer, without unit suffix. Zero adds no context. Counts apply separately before and after each match; overlapping groups are merged. Overflow saturates at the implementation's intmax_t maximum instead of imposing a smaller guessed fixed limit.

special_values.meaning: Do not add surrounding context lines

when_absent.meaning: Add no surrounding context through this option.

options.summary: List files with no selected lines
options.detail: Use -L to list each input that would produce no selected lines. Exit status still tracks selection across all inputs. A listed file alone can give status 1. Use -Z for NUL-terminated names.

options.summary: Stop successfully at the first selected line
options.detail: Use -q or --silent for a status-only search. File errors can still produce diagnostics. A selected line gives status 0 even after an earlier file error.

options.summary: Suppress diagnostics for missing or unreadable files
options.detail: Use -s to hide file-access errors. Matches still print and a file error normally gives status 2. Use -q to stop successfully as soon as a line is selected.

options.summary: Limit selected lines per input file
options.detail: Use -m NUM per file. With -v, count selected nonmatching lines. Omit -m for an unlimited inverted search. Explicit -m -1 can suppress all its output on both Ubuntu builds. Zero normally exits before reading input, but -m0 -L still examines file names. A positive limit allows trailing context. On regular-file standard input grep leaves the stream just after the last selected line.

forms.grammar: A decimal integer counts lines, without a unit suffix. The manual specifies nonnegative counts and the special value -1. The signed parser saturates on overflow.

special_values.meaning: Documented as unlimited. With -v on the tested Ubuntu builds omit -m instead.

options.summary: Prefix output with zero-based byte offsets
options.detail: With -b, the offset is the start of the line in its input file. With -o, it is the first byte of each printed match. A multibyte character can occupy several bytes.

options.summary: Prefix output with the input file name
options.detail: Use -H to force a name even for a single file or standard input. Multiple input files normally get prefixes automatically. Use --label to name standard input.

options.summary: Omit file names from line prefixes
options.detail: Use -h when searching several files or a directory tree. A single file or standard input normally has no prefix. Filename-list modes still print names.

options.summary: Set the displayed name for standard input
options.detail: Use -H to show the label when searching a pipeline alone. The label is a display name and does not open a file.

options.summary: Align the start of output text to a tab stop
options.detail: Use -T with prefixes such as -H, -n or -b to keep tabs in the line content aligned. Numbers and offsets may be padded with spaces.

options.summary: Terminate each printed file name with NUL
options.detail: With -Z, a filename prefix ends in NUL instead of its separator. With -l or -L, each listed name ends in NUL, even if the name contains a newline. Matched lines and -o matches still end in newline unless -z is also set.

options.summary: Read and print NUL-delimited records
options.detail: With -z, newlines are ordinary input bytes. Printed records and each -o match end in NUL. Filename lists (-l or -L) still use newline unless -Z is set. When an input has no NUL, grep may need to hold the entire file in memory.

options.summary: Show lines after each selected line
options.detail: Use -A NUM for trailing context. Its count overrides the trailing side of -C. Adjacent or overlapping groups print once. With -o, surrounding lines are omitted.

forms.grammar: Nonnegative decimal integer in lines, without a unit suffix. Positive overflow saturates at the maximum value of intmax_t.

when_absent.meaning: Use the both-sides context setting, or zero when no context was requested.

options.detail: Use -a for --binary-files=text. Matching lines can contain raw control bytes. Redirect output if these bytes are unsuitable for a terminal.

options.summary: Treat unprocessed binary data as nonmatching
